t: Largest Values From Labels — Greedy with Sorting and Label Counting
o: We must pick at most `numWanted` items, never taking more than `useLimit` items sharing the same label, to maximize the total value. Since every item has a non-negative value, taking an item never hurts — so we should always prefer higher-valued items. Walk through Example 1: sorted by value descending gives (5,label 1),(4,1),(3,2),(2,2),(1,3); with useLimit=1 we take 5 (label 1 used), skip 4, take 3 (label 2), take 1 (label 3) → sum 9. Example 2: take 5, take 4 (label 3 count 1), take 3 (label 3 count 2) → 12. Example 3: take 9, skip both 8s (label 0 exhausted), take 7 → 16. Constraints ($n \le 2\cdot10^4$) allow $O(n \log n)$ sorting easily; a brute force over subsets is exponential and unnecessary.
k: All values are non-negative, so a greedy exchange argument works: swapping any chosen item for a higher-valued unchosen one never violates constraints.
Sort items by value descending and greedily take items while tracking per-label usage counts.
Stop early once numWanted items are taken.

a.i: Enumerate all subsets of items, check each against the two constraints, and track the maximum sum. This directly mirrors the problem definition but is exponential in n, so it only serves as a conceptual baseline for tiny inputs.
s: Iterate over all 2^n subsets via bitmask.
For each subset, verify size <= numWanted and each label's count <= useLimit.
If valid, update the answer with the subset's value sum.
a.t: O(2^n · n) — enumerating all subsets and checking each.

a.n: Approach 2: Greedy — Sort by Value Descending with Hash-Map Counting (Optimal)
a.i: Because all values are non-negative, a greedy strategy is provably optimal: process items from highest to lowest value and take each item unless its label has already been used useLimit times or we already have numWanted items. Any optimal solution can be transformed into this greedy one by exchanging lower-valued picks for higher-valued skipped ones without breaking constraints.
s: Build index pairs (value, label) and sort by value descending.
Maintain a hash map counting how many times each label was used.
Scan sorted items; take an item if its label count < useLimit and total picked < numWanted, adding its value and incrementing the count.
Stop early once numWanted items are taken.
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the scan is O(n) with O(1) hash-map operations.
a.sp: O(n) — for the item pairs and the label-count hash map.

w: In an interview, go straight to the greedy approach after noting that non-negative values make it safe — mention the exchange argument briefly to justify correctness. Common pitfalls: forgetting the early stop at numWanted (harmless but wasteful), miscounting label usage when equal values tie (order among ties doesn't matter since any valid pick yields the same sum), and off-by-one errors on useLimit checks. Edge cases: numWanted >= n (take everything subject to useLimit), useLimit = 1 (at most one item per label), and all items sharing one label. Follow-ups might ask for O(n log n) without full sort (bucket/counting sort since values ≤ 2·10^4), or handling negative values, which would break the naive greedy and require rethinking.
